This one’s a classic counting permutation series with dynamic programming. We know we’re looking at all possible permutations starting from each unique character, so let's break down the approach into manageable chunks.

Our goal is to find total possibilities as sum(S!). 
In other words, how many strings can you make using the characters of String S?

To achieve this, use dynamic programming where dp[i] represents the number of ways to form i-character strings (i.e., sub-sequences). Since we can reuse any char once its used up before, add them incrementally according to their counts. At last, return sum(dp) % M

Time complexity O(2**n), space O(1).
For loop through each input element & multiply the frequency count with remaining elements.
We're multiplying frequencies because a pair like 'xy' contributes to both xy and yx. It makes sense mathematically, but why not see it intuitively?
For e.g.: ‘aab’ has two sub sequences : “” & "a". So how did our output go from “18”, “54”, “108”? A closer look will reveal that 108 was divided equally among "a", "bb".

At first glance, there appears to be double-counting here, but actually it follows naturally from how Python handles duplicates during concatenation.

With more than one letter, duplicate pairs such as (‘aab’, ‘abb’) come together and share factors leading towards a balanced distribution throughout our final product.
So instead of adding twice, we divide each calculated factor by 2!
